name: Semaglutide
heroIntro: Explore compounded semaglutide as a potential treatment option through an online evaluation with a licensed healthcare provider.
cardBlurb: A GLP-1 option that may support weight management when prescribed by a licensed provider.
what: Semaglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that acts on receptors involved in appetite regulation and blood glucose control.
Compounded semaglutide is a prescription medication prepared by a licensed compounding pharmacy for an individual patient when prescribed by a healthcare provider.
Compounded semaglutide is not FDA-approved and is not an FDA-approved generic equivalent of any brand-name medication.
Your provider will determine whether this treatment is medically appropriate for you.
photoAlt: Smiling middle-aged couple outdoors in warm sunlight

isi.boxed: In studies in rodents, semaglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumors. It is not known whether semaglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans. Do not use semaglutide if you or any of your family members have ever had MTC, or if you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Tell your healthcare provider right away if you develop a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.
doNotUse: You or a family member have ever had medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
You have had a serious allergic reaction to semaglutide or any of the ingredients in your medication.
You are using another product that contains semaglutide or another GLP-1 receptor agonist.
serious: Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis). Stop using and call your provider right away if you have severe stomach pain that will not go away, with or without vomiting.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), particularly when used with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
Kidney problems, including kidney failure, which can be caused by dehydration from nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious allergic reactions, including swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, or severe rash.
Changes in vision in people with type 2 diabetes.
Depression or thoughts of suicide. Call your provider right away if you have new or worsening mood changes.
Food or liquid getting into the lungs during surgery or procedures that use anesthesia or deep sedation. Tell all of your providers that you use semaglutide before any procedure.
isi.common: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, headache, fatigue, upset stomach, dizziness, bloating, belching, gas, and heartburn.
isi.pregnancy: Tell your provider if you are pregnant, plan to become pregnant, or are breastfeeding. Semaglutide may harm an unborn baby.
isi.tellProvider: Tell your provider about all medical conditions and medications, including any history of diabetic retinopathy, planned procedures requiring anesthesia or deep sedation, pregnancy, or breastfeeding.

administration: Compounded semaglutide injection may be prescribed for subcutaneous administration, generally once weekly.
Your provider and dispensing pharmacy will supply instructions specific to your prescription, including dose, concentration, injection technique, and schedule.

Compounded products may have different concentrations. Always follow the exact instructions on your prescription label. Do not substitute syringe units for milligrams without confirming the conversion with your pharmacist.

name: Tirzepatide
heroIntro: Explore compounded tirzepatide as a potential treatment option with licensed healthcare providers through TAM Longevity.
cardBlurb: A dual-acting treatment option that may support weight management when prescribed by a licensed provider.
what: Tirzepatide acts on two hormone receptor pathways involved in metabolic regulation: glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1).
Compounded tirzepatide is a prescription medication prepared by a licensed compounding pharmacy for an individual patient when prescribed by a healthcare provider.
Compounded tirzepatide is not FDA-approved and is not an FDA-approved generic equivalent of a brand-name medication.
Your provider will evaluate whether treatment is appropriate based on your medical history and individual needs.

isi.boxed: In studies in rodents, tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumors. It is not known whether tirzepatide causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans. Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family members have ever had MTC, or if you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Tell your healthcare provider right away if you develop a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.
doNotUse: You or a family member have ever had medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

You are using another product that contains tirzepatide or a GLP-1 receptor agonist.
serious: Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis). Stop using and call your provider right away if you have severe stomach pain that will not go away, with or without vomiting.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), particularly when used with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
Kidney problems, including kidney failure, which can be caused by dehydration from nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious allergic reactions, including swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, or severe rash.
Depression or thoughts of suicide. Call your provider right away if you have new or worsening mood changes.
Food or liquid getting into the lungs during surgery or procedures that use anesthesia or deep sedation. Tell all of your providers that you use tirzepatide before any procedure.
isi.common: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal discomfort, indigestion, injection-site reactions, fatigue, allergic reactions, belching, hair loss, and heartburn.
isi.pregnancy: Tell your provider if you are pregnant, plan to become pregnant, or are breastfeeding. Tirzepatide may harm an unborn baby. Birth control pills taken by mouth may not work as well while using tirzepatide; your provider may recommend a non-oral method for 4 weeks after you start and for 4 weeks after each dose increase.
isi.tellProvider: Tell your provider if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, breastfeeding, have a history of significant gastrointestinal disease, or have a planned procedure involving anesthesia or deep sedation. Tirzepatide can affect absorption of oral medications.
